title: How do you design a production backup strategy — frequency (daily full + continuous WAL archiving), retention policy, off-site/cross-region copies, automated restore testing, RTO/RPO targets?

s1_definition.profdef: A production backup strategy is a documented plan that ties backup frequency, retention, storage location, and verification to business recovery targets — the Recovery Point Objective (how much data you can afford to lose) and the Recovery Time Objective (how fast you must be back). A typical design is daily full base backups plus continuous WAL archiving, tiered retention, cross-region off-site copies, and automated restore drills.
s1_definition.analogy: For National Bank of India, this is the bank's whole insurance policy for its data: how often it photographs the vault, how long it keeps old photographs, where it stores duplicates so one fire cannot destroy them all, and regular fire drills to prove it can actually reopen the vault. It is driven by two promises — lose at most a few seconds of data, and be back within an hour.
s1_definition.oneliner: Design backups backward from RPO and RTO: daily full plus continuous WAL, tiered retention, cross-region copies, and tested restores.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A production backup strategy is a documented plan that ties backup frequency, retention, storage location, and verification to business recovery targets — the Recovery Point Objective (how much data you can afford to lose) and the Recovery Time Objective (how fast you must be back). A typical design is daily full base backups plus continuous WAL archiving, tiered retention, cross-region off-site copies, and automated restore drills.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** For National Bank of India, this is the bank's whole insurance policy for its data: how often it photographs the vault, how long it keeps old photographs, where it stores duplicates so one fire cannot destroy them all, and regular fire drills to prove it can actually reopen the vault. It is driven by two promises — lose at most a few seconds of data, and be back within an hour.

**One line to remember:** Design backups backward from RPO and RTO: daily full plus continuous WAL, tiered retention, cross-region copies, and tested restores.

sections.s2_technical:
Start from targets. The Recovery Point Objective fixes backup frequency: if you can lose at most seconds, you need continuous WAL archiving on top of periodic full backups; if minutes to an hour, less frequent increments suffice. The Recovery Time Objective fixes the restore method: tight RTO favors fast physical restores and warm standbys over slow logical replays.

Frequency: daily full base backup plus continuous WAL archiving gives point-in-time recovery between fulls. Retention: tier it — keep hourly/daily for a short window, weekly for a month, monthly for a year or as regulation requires (banks often must keep years). Storage: follow the 3-2-1 idea — multiple copies, more than one medium, at least one off-site, and for cloud at least one cross-region copy so a regional outage does not lose everything; encrypt at rest and in transit.

Verification: automate restore tests on a schedule into a scratch environment and alert on failure, because an untested backup is a hope, not a plan. Also monitor archive continuity (no WAL gaps), backup success, and backup age.

Senior nuance: document and rehearse the runbook so RTO is measured, not guessed; protect backups from the same blast radius (separate credentials, immutable/object-lock storage to resist ransomware); and align retention with compliance and privacy rules, including the ability to purge specific data.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India must guarantee near-zero data loss and fast recovery for its ledger while meeting retention regulations. This is exactly a full strategy: schedule fulls plus WAL, tier retention, replicate cross-region, and test restores automatically.

The demo has a `BackupPolicy` capturing RPO/RTO, frequency, and retention, and a `BackupOrchestrator` that schedules fulls and increments, enforces retention, copies cross-region, and runs a restore drill, logging each step.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__backup_catalog.sql (tracks backups + verification outcomes)
CREATE TABLE backup_catalog (
    id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    kind        VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,        -- FULL / WAL / RESTORE_TEST
    taken_at    TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    location    VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,       -- s3 primary + cross-region
    verified    BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE,
    expires_at  TIMESTAMP NOT NULL           -- retention policy
);
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
backup-strategy:
  rpo-seconds: 5            # continuous WAL archiving
  rto-minutes: 60
  full: { schedule: "daily" }
  wal: { mode: continuous }
  retention: { daily: 7, weekly: 4, monthly: 84 }   # 7 years monthly for compliance
  storage:
    primary: s3://nbi-backups-mumbai/
    cross-region: s3://nbi-backups-delhi/           # off-site copy
    object-lock: true                               # ransomware resistance
  restore-test: { schedule: "weekly", target: scratch-db }
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a policy of 5-second RPO, 60-minute RTO, 7 daily and 84 monthly retentions.

Step 1: runDailyFull takes the base backup and immediately copies it to the cross-region off-site bucket, while continuous WAL archiving keeps the RPO at seconds.

Step 2: enforceRetention prunes anything past its tier, keeping seven dailies and seven years of monthlies for compliance.

Step 3: restoreDrill measures an actual recovery (42 minutes) and confirms it is within the 60-minute RTO, proving the plan works.

```text
2026-10-25 18:38:00 [INFO] FULL base backup taken; RPO=5s via continuous WAL
2026-10-25 18:38:00 [INFO] copied full to cross-region bucket (off-site, object-lock)
2026-10-25 18:38:00 [INFO] retention: keep daily=7, monthly=84 months; expired pruned
2026-10-25 18:38:00 [INFO] RESTORE DRILL OK: recovered in 42m (RTO=60m)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
I design a production backup strategy backward from the business recovery targets. The Recovery Point Objective — how much data we can afford to lose — sets the frequency, and for a bank that is near zero, so I run daily full base backups plus continuous write-ahead-log archiving to give point-in-time recovery between fulls. The Recovery Time Objective — how fast we must be back — sets the method, favoring fast physical restores and warm standbys over slow logical replays.

In our National Bank of India platform the retention is tiered — a week of dailies, a month of weeklies, and years of monthlies to satisfy regulation — and every backup follows the three-two-one principle with an encrypted cross-region off-site copy on object-lock storage so neither a regional outage nor ransomware can destroy all copies. The part I insist on is automated verification: a scheduled restore drill into a scratch environment that actually measures the recovery time against the Recovery Time Objective and alerts on failure, because an untested backup is only a hope. I also monitor archive continuity so there are no write-ahead-log gaps, keep backup credentials separate from production to limit blast radius, and rehearse the documented runbook so the recovery time is measured rather than guessed. The line I remember is: design backups backward from RPO and RTO — daily full plus continuous WAL, tiered retention, cross-region copies, and tested restores.
